raw_response:
My land here in Quzhou has been growing wheat and maize my whole life, and my mother's before that. I am 67 now, my back is not what it was, and two of my children work in Shijiazhuang. I have about 7 mu of flat field. There is no reason to change what I know.

In autumn I will sow winter wheat, same as always. I buy the seed from the village supply store — the kind they recommend there, not the old varieties, those yield less. I will rotary-till before sowing because that is what our machines here do. For fertilizer I will put down diammonium phosphate and some urea when I sow, then add more urea in spring when the wheat starts to stretch. I will irrigate three times: once before winter sets in, once at jointing, once when the heads come out. I will spray twice — herbicide in spring, and something for aphids and rust near heading time if I see them, which I usually do.

After the wheat comes off in June I will plant maize right away on the same ground. I always buy hybrid seed — my neighbor switched years ago and I saw the difference, I am not going back to the old seed for maize. No tilling, just direct seeding into the stubble. The summer rains help but Quzhou is dry, so I will water twice. I will fertilize at planting and again when the maize is knee-high. Spray twice for pests and corn borer.

I will keep a small patch near the house for garlic and cabbage for ourselves, but I do not count that as a plan — it is just the garden.

decision.reasoning_summary: I farm 7 mu of flat land in Quzhou County the same way it has been farmed for generations: winter wheat followed immediately by summer maize on the same ground. I use improved wheat seed from the village store and hybrid maize seed because the yield difference is real and I have seen it myself. I apply fertilizer at sowing and topdress in season, irrigate three times for wheat and twice for maize given how dry Quzhou is, and spray twice each crop for the weeds and insects that always come. I rotary-till before wheat but go no-till into the stubble for maize because the machines make it easy and it saves my back. These are the crops and methods I know, my body can still manage them with some hired help at harvest, and they give me and my family enough grain to sell and to eat.
